General.Description:
Lorenzo Mazzini (1471–1539) painted seventeen surviving works. Art historians rank at least nine of them among the finest productions of the High Renaissance. He is almost entirely unknown outside specialist circles, and has no entry in most popular reference works on the period. This biography sets out to explain why — and to right that historical wrong.

Giulia Esposito, herself a professor of Renaissance art history at the University of Bologna, spent fifteen years tracing the arc of Mazzini's career through parish records, guild archives, private letters, and the physical evidence hidden in the works themselves. What she found was a painter of astonishing technical innovation who spent most of his career in the deliberate shadow of more famous contemporaries, using anonymity as both protection and creative freedom.

The Painter's Eye reconstructs a man who chose obscurity with the same intentionality with which others sought fame — and examines what that choice cost him, and what it freed him to paint. Esposito's analysis of individual works is penetrating and accessible to non-specialist readers, and her recreation of daily life in early sixteenth-century Florence is vivid and deeply researched.

A revelation of a book.
